purpose: Chlorhexidine is used to kill germs and bacteria on the skin or in the mouth. As a mouth rinse, it helps treat gum disease and reduce mouth infections. As a skin wash or surgical scrub, it cleans and disinfects the skin before procedures or surgeries.
how_it_works: Chlorhexidine works by attacking the outer layer of bacteria cells, causing them to break apart and die. It sticks to surfaces in your mouth or on your skin for a long time, so it keeps killing germs even after you rinse or wash. This long-lasting effect makes it especially helpful for preventing infections.
common_side_effects: When used as a mouth rinse, it can stain your teeth, tongue, or dental work brown or yellow over time. You may also notice a temporary change in your sense of taste. When used on skin, it can sometimes cause mild irritation, dryness, or redness in sensitive people.
warnings: Do not swallow the mouth rinse — it is only meant to be swished and spit out. Keep it away from your ears, as it can cause hearing damage if it gets inside the ear canal. Avoid contact with your eyes. Some people may have a rare but serious allergic reaction — tell your doctor right away if you notice rash, swelling, or trouble breathing. Let your dentist know if you use it regularly, so they can monitor for tooth staining.
typical_dosing: For the mouth rinse, the usual dose is about half a tablespoon (15 mL) swished around your mouth for 30 seconds, then spit out — typically twice a day after brushing your teeth. For skin use, apply to the area as directed by your doctor or nurse, usually before a medical procedure. Always follow the exact instructions given to you by your healthcare provider.
